context: The deque is on the left and its underlying circular array is drawn vertically on the right. Both run from front to rear down the page. The variable front holds the front index, and size counts the active elements. Moving up one slot decreases the index by 1, corresponding to “move left” in the code comments. Moving down one slot increases the index by 1.

The next write position at the rear is rear = (front + size) % capacity. The figure uses the shorter rear = front + size. It shows no wraparound and gives neither a specific capacity nor numeric indices.
description: Enqueueing requires a free slot, and dequeueing requires a nonempty deque. The active elements occupy indices (front + i) % capacity, where i ranges from 0 through size - 1. To enqueue at the front, update front to (front - 1 + capacity) % capacity.

The original elements 3, 2, and 5 stay in their slots throughout. Gray dashed cells mark slots outside the active range. A dashed outline after removal does not mean the code cleared the old value. The new rear element, 4, is teal, and the new front element, 1, is orange.

frames.announcement: The active deque starts as [3, 2, 5], with front pointing to 3 and size = 3. The rear index points to the first empty slot after 5.
frames.explanation: The active deque starts as [3, 2, 5], with front pointing to 3 and size = 3. Calculating rear as front + size gives the first empty slot below 5. Empty slots and ellipses appear at both ends of the array.
frames.key_state: The active deque is [3, 2, 5], front points to 3, and size = 3. The rear index points to the empty slot below 5.
frames.title: Initial deque

frames.announcement: Write 4 at the rear index calculated before insertion and increase size to 4. The rear arrow in the figure stays at the newly written 4.
frames.explanation: The call push_last(4) first calculates rear using front and the old size of 3. It writes 4 into that empty slot, then increases size to 4. The deque is now [3, 2, 5, 4], and front still points to 3. The figure leaves the rear arrow at the newly written 4. Recalculating rear with the new size would put it one slot below 4.
frames.key_state: The front index points to 3, size = 4, and the active deque is [3, 2, 5, 4]. The rear marker in the figure shows where 4 was written.
frames.title: Add 4 at the rear

frames.announcement: Move front up one slot, write 1 there, and increase size to 5. All other elements stay in place.
frames.explanation: The call push_first(1) moves front up one slot to the empty slot above 3, writes 1 there, and increases size from 4 to 5. The deque is now [1, 3, 2, 5, 4]. The front index points to the new first element, 1, and all the others stay in their slots. This frame has no rear marker.
frames.key_state: The front index points to 1, size = 5, and the active deque is [1, 3, 2, 5, 4].
frames.title: Add 1 at the front

frames.announcement: Read and return the rear element, 4, and reduce size to 4. The old rear slot leaves the active range.
frames.explanation: The call pop_last() reads and returns the rear element, 4, and reduces size from 5 to 4. The deque is now [1, 3, 2, 5], and front still points to 1. The slot that held 4 now has a dashed outline because it is outside the active range. This frame has no rear marker.
frames.key_state: The front index points to 1, size = 4, and the active deque is [1, 3, 2, 5]. The call returns 4.
frames.title: Remove 4 from the rear

frames.announcement: Read and return the front element, 1. Move front down one slot to point to 3 again and reduce size to 3.
frames.explanation: The call pop_first() reads and returns the front element, 1, moves front down one slot to point to 3 again, and reduces size from 4 to 3. The deque is back to [3, 2, 5], and the slot that held 1 is outside the active range. This frame has no rear marker.
frames.key_state: The front index points to 3, size = 3, and the active deque is [3, 2, 5]. The call returns 1.
frames.title: Remove 1 from the front

result: Insertion and removal at either end update only an end slot, front, or size. The middle elements stay in place, so all four operations take O(1) time.
summary: Tracking the front index and the number of active elements lets us operate at either end without shifting the elements in between.
title: Implementing a deque with a circular array
